title: WHAT IF YOU HIT AN ASTEROID
AT 14,000 MPH?

sets.launch: Vandenberg launch pad at night. far: SpaceBackdrop #0A0A1E with first stars; mid: a tall white-silver rocket on a dark gantry with floodlight bloom; near: dark GroundPlane with pale rim. setp.t 0..1 = liftoff (0 on the pad, 1 gone up with a long orange flame and smoke); setp.tint 'night'.
sets.cruise: Deep space in motion. SpaceBackdrop #0A0A1E with star streaks flowing past; a tiny bright dot ahead that grows with setp.t 0..1 (0 = a speck, 1 = a big grey rock filling the right third); faint cream dotted trajectory line from the left edge to the dot; setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'.
sets.binary: The Didymos pair. far: SpaceBackdrop with sparse stars; mid: a big lumpy grey asteroid (Didymos, 780 m) with a clear ridge around its equator, boulders and craters, pale rim light from the left; a much smaller grey moonlet (Dimorphos, 151 m) orbiting it. setp.t 0..1 = moonlet position along its orbit; setp.zoom 0..1 = closeness (0 both small, 1 filling the frame); setp.dart 0..1 = a tiny spacecraft approaching Dimorphos from the left (1 = touching).
sets.impact: Impact close-up. A grey boulder-strewn asteroid surface fills the lower half; at setp.t 0 a small spacecraft with two gold solar panels streaks in from the left; 0.4 white-gold flash; then a cone of dust and rocks sprays up and out to the right with long tail streaks. setp.t 0..1 = the sequence; setp.debris 0..1 = amount of ejecta.
sets.orbitdiag: Top-down orbit diagram. Deep-navy backdrop; the big asteroid Didymos as a grey disc at centre, a thin cream orbit ring around it with the small moonlet dot; a second, slightly smaller gold ring for the new orbit. setp.t 0..1 = moonlet moves round; setp.shift 0..1 = the cream ring shrinks to the gold ring with an arrow; setp.glow 0|1 = gold glow on the new ring.
sets.hera: Hera surveying Didymos. far: SpaceBackdrop; mid: a huge grey lumpy asteroid with ridge, boulders, craters and groove patterns filling the right two thirds; near: a small ESA spacecraft (white body, two blue-grey solar panels, a small camera eye) on the left. setp.t 0..1 = spacecraft drifts closer; setp.side 0|1 = 0 shows the side DART saw (smooth with ridge), 1 shows the new side (boulders, craters, grooves); setp.scan 0..1 = a cyan scan line sweeps across.
sets.ops: Mission operations room. far: wall of dark screens with glowing cream trajectory curves; mid: rows of desks, headset lamps, no faces; near: carpet GroundPlane with pale rim. setp.tension 0..1 = number of screens flashing amber; setp.ok 1 turns all screens green with a soft pulse.
sets.earthview: Earth and a danger rock. Deep-navy space; a blue Earth with pale rim at left; a cream dotted path with a grey asteroid approaching from the right; setp.t 0..1 = asteroid distance (1 near Earth); setp.nudge 0..1 = a small spacecraft hits it and the dotted path bends away from Earth.
sets.void: Plain deep-navy SpaceBackdrop stage with slow light rays and almost no stars, for big numbers, bars and diagrams. setp.glow 'gold'|'cyan'|'red' tints the rays.

props.dart: Small DART spacecraft icon: a small boxy silver body with two long gold solar-array wings, a tiny camera eye on the front, 4 px dark outline, soft rim light; pp.flame true adds a thin blue thruster glow; pp.s scale.
props.hera: Small ESA Hera icon: white boxy body, two blue-grey solar panels, a small camera eye; 4 px outline; pp.s scale.
props.rock: Small lumpy grey asteroid icon with craters, 4 px outline, pale rim; pp.moon true adds a smaller rock circling it; pp.label text beneath.
props.counter: Big flat panel, 4 px dark outline, dark #1E1B2E face, cream flip digits in FONTS.title with thousands separators, label in FONTS.ui underneath. pp.from and pp.to: the number counts from->to across the shot (ease-out); pp.label text; pp.color gold|red|cyan.
props.clock: Round analogue clock face, cream disc, 4 px dark outline, ticks, one hand. pp.from..pp.to in hours: the hand sweeps; pp.glow true adds a gold bloom.
props.stopwatch: Round outlined stopwatch, cream face, red button on top; pp.from..pp.to minutes: hand sweeps and digits count.
props.bar: Horizontal progress bar with 4 px outline, filled with pp.color (gold|red|cyan) to pp.frac of its width over the shot; pp.label above in FONTS.ui.
props.arrow: Thick outlined curved arrow, pp.color gold|cyan|red, draws on across the shot.
props.flag: Small green check mark badge in a round outlined cream disc with a tiny sparkle; or red cross when pp.bad true.
props.sign: Hand-painted sign on a post, cream board, dark outline, pp.text in FONTS.hand (max 12 chars).
props.calendar: Small wall calendar page, cream with a red top strip, 4 px outline; pp.text the date in FONTS.title (max 8 chars).

actions.lookup: Pip tilts head back (headTilt up), arms hang loose, small sway; eyes lift at p 0.2.
actions.duck: Pip drops into a crouch with both arms raised over the head at p 0.15 and holds with a small tremble.
actions.spin: Pip turns one slow full rotation (yaw/spin) across the shot while looking up.
actions.flinch: A quick squash and lean away at p 0.2 with arms up, then settles back by p 0.7.
actions.pointup: Pip's arm swings up to point at the sky at p 0.2 with a small overshoot.

film.vo: Fourteen thousand miles an hour. One rock. No brakes.
You are the spacecraft.
Five hundred eighty kilograms. Smaller than a car.
Your target is a moonlet one hundred fifty-one metres wide.
Hit it, and you change the sky.
Miss, and you are just a very fast rock.
This really happened. NASA did it on the twenty-sixth of September.
So what if you rode that spacecraft into an asteroid?
Here are the rules.
You can steer a little. You can never stop.
There are two asteroids, not one.
Didymos is the big one. Seven hundred eighty metres.
Dimorphos is its little moon. You are aiming at the moon.
They sit only about one kilometre apart.
The moon circles the big rock, over and over.
Your goal is simple. Make that loop shorter.
By crashing into it. On purpose.
Nobody had ever tried it. Now, you go.
First, you need a ride.
A Falcon Nine rocket, on the twenty-third of November, twenty twenty-one.
Ten twenty-one at night, from California.
Three. Two. One.
And you rise.
Then the rocket lets go. You are alone.
Your wings unfold. Gold, glittering, enormous.
There is a long way to go.
Ten months of nothing but stars.
Your calendar flips. And flips. And flips.
Then something appears ahead. A speck.
That speck is home. Your target.
It is September, twenty twenty-two. The speck grows.
Now it is two rocks. A big one and a small one.
Your camera locks onto the small one.
The last seconds are all yours.
Home is a very long way behind you.
Every correction is yours to make, alone.
One bad nudge, and you sail past.
The moon fills your view. A hundred and fifty-one metres of boulders.
You can see the shadows now. Every crater.
You are going six point one kilometres every second.
That is more than twenty-one thousand kilometres an hour.
Fourteen thousand miles an hour, if you like miles.
Ten seconds out. The ground is a wall of rock.
Three. Two. One.
Contact.
Your five hundred eighty kilograms hit like a hammer made of speed.
Dust and rock fly out into space.
A long tail of debris, streaming away from the moon.
Mission control goes silent.
Then the room erupts.
You hit. But did it move?
Nobody can see the moon move. It is too far.
So scientists wait, and time its orbit.
Before the hit, one loop took a certain time.
Now the stopwatch is running again.
And the answer is coming.
The moon's orbit got shorter by thirty-three minutes.
Give or take one minute.
That was far more than scientists expected.
Thirty-three minutes. That is a whole episode of a sitcom.
You shoved a rock, and the rock moved.
No one had ever done that to a world before.
The first object in the Solar System we measurably nudged.
Think about that. A spacecraft smaller than a car.
Moved a rock a hundred and fifty metres wide.
But the story does not end there.
Four years later, a visitor arrives to survey the damage.
Meet Hera. A European spacecraft.
Its job is a crash site investigation.
It took two years to get there.
It sits one hundred ninety-six million kilometres from Earth.
This week it sent back a picture.
It shows Didymos, the big rock, from a side no one had seen.
DART's camera only ever saw the other face.
The first thing the Hera scientists said was wow.
It has the same ridge around its middle.
But everything else looks different.
Boulders. Craters. Strange grooves and ridges.
Here is the mystery. Did your crash cause some of it?
The debris you kicked up may have crossed one kilometre of space.
And landed on Didymos. Scarring it.
Hera will map every change.
Next reveal: the twenty-fifth of November.
Why does any of this matter?
One day, an asteroid might be heading for Earth.
A hit like yours could nudge it away.
It is called kinetic impact deflection.
DART proved it works once.
Hera helps scientists make it work every time.
A one-off demo becomes a dependable shield.
And it all started with a little spacecraft.
Remember that fourteen thousand miles an hour?
Now you know where it ends. A rock, a shove, a new orbit.
Tomorrow: what if you flew straight into the Sun?
Which world would you crash into first? Tell me below.

short.vo: You are flying at fourteen thousand miles an hour.
There are no brakes. Only a rock.
You are NASA's DART. Five hundred eighty kilograms.
Your target is a moon, one hundred fifty-one metres wide.
You hit it on purpose, on the twenty-sixth of September.
And that shoved the moon's orbit shorter by thirty-three minutes.
First time humans moved an asteroid's orbit.
Now Europe's Hera is there, looking at the crash site.
It just found a side of Didymos nobody has seen.
Boulders. Craters. Grooves. Maybe scars from your crash.
That is how we learn to push a killer rock away.
Full film on the channel. Tomorrow: what if you flew into the Sun?
